episodes.212398: Clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms dropped southeast into southern middle Tennessee and north Alabama during the afternoon and early evening hours.  Damaging winds were reported in northwest Alabama including the Shoals metro area.
episodes.212437: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) track southeast through western portions of Middle Tennessee during the morning hours of June 1, 2026. This MCS was mainly non-severe, but a more favorable environment near the Tennessee and Alabama border caused it to strengthen, producing sporadic damaging winds. A few trees or tree branches were reported down across portions of southwest Middle Tennessee.
episodes.212438: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.
episodes.212470: Isolated strong storms produced high winds, hail and flooding in portions of northeast South Dakota. Hail to the size of quarters was recorded 6 miles southeast of the town of Roscoe and near the town of Leola. Additionally, winds were estimated at 60 mph 5 miles north northeast of Leola, with a 59 mph peak wind recorded on the Sand Lake RAWS. The primary impact of these storms was the heavy rainfall around the Leola area. The SDSU mesonet station on the east side of Leola recorded 5.48 inches of moisture with this system. Flooding in the town of Leola impacted many residents with street and basement flooding. 6 to 12 inches of water was observed covering portions of Highway 10 just west of town and heavy equipment was required to move water and debris. Highway 45 south of town was also impassible due to flooding.
episodes.212485: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
episodes.212523: Intense daytime heating resulted in the development of a dust devil in a Rio Rancho neighborhood during the mid afternoon. Video shared by local media showed the dust devil resulted in some minor damage.
episodes.212681: Very hot temperatures and a dryline allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon of the 31st. Thunderstorms initially developed along this dryline from the northern Rolling Plains into the southern South Plains. The thunderstorms gradually grew upscale into a broken, slow moving line that persisted over the central Rolling Plains into the south-central South Plains through the evening hours. These slow moving thunderstorms primarily produced torrential rainfall but also large hail and damaging wind gusts. Excessive runoff from the prolonged heavy rain flooded fields and inundated area roadways. Some of the heaviest rainfall was along US Highway 87 north of Tahoka in Lynn County. Water over the roadway and a water rescue prompted the closure of the highway. Several additional vehicles became flooded out along US Highway 87. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 west of Post (Garza County) and in northwestern Lubbock (Lubbock County). As storms decreased in intensity late in the evening, a couple of wake lows formed producing severe wind gusts near Slaton (Lubbock County) and Paducah (Cottle County).
episodes.212701: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.
episodes.213126: Scattered thunderstorms developed on the nose of a low level jet during the very early morning of June 1st. As they approached central Missouri, these thunderstorms congealed into a mesoscale convective complex. This complex produced wind damage extending from Boone County through Washington County, and produced flash flooding in Columbia.
episodes.213163: A severe thunderstorm occurred during the afternoon of June 1 in Douglas County with large hail.
episodes.213421: A few supercells developed across portions of central and east-central Kansas during the night of May 31. These storms produced half-dollar to golf ball size hail. There was also a brief tornado near the town of Madison, Kansas.
episodes.213441: To close out the month, several supercells developed across east-central KS on the evening of May 31. These supercells produced hail in excess of baseball size.
episodes.213631: Active start of the month with large hail and strong winds across far eastern Wyoming during the afternoon. Some flash flooding also reported in Platte and Goshen County.
episodes.213744: Showers and thunderstorms affected the combined Panhandles each afternoon and evening in the early parts of June. With enough moisture, instability and sources to provide atmospheric lift, these storms were able to become severe each day and bring large hail to the region. A few instances of damaging winds and flooding also occurred.
episodes.213760: During the late evening hours of May 31 and into the early morning of June 1, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped across northeast Nebraska and western Iowa became the focal point for strong to severe thunderstorm development. The environment along the boundary featured roughly 2,000 J/kg of instability and 30 knots of deep-layer shear, which proved sufficient to organize convection. Additionally, a dry sub-cloud layer yielded approximately 1,400 J/kg of DCAPE, promoting a severe downdraft threat alongside the hail risk.||As storms initiated and pushed southward overnight, radar signatures indicated the potential for several swaths of large hail and damaging winds, particularly across western Iowa. However, because the storms primarily traversed sparsely populated areas late at night, only a handful of severe weather reports were received. Quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail was estimated near the towns of Woodbine and Avoca, Iowa. The storms also produced a measured wind gust of 63 mph and localized tree damage in Pottawattamie County, Iowa. The complex continued tracking southward, eventually decreasing in intensity and weakening below severe limits during the early morning hours.

episodes.213902: Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the early evening of the 1st. The strongest storms produced large hail up to quarter size.
episodes.214278: An approaching frontal boundary to the Natural State at the beginning of the episode would become a stationary boundary as the upper level flow pattern would begin as an approaching positively-tilted trough axis which would become an omega block and lock the mesoscale feature of the stationary boundary in position across Arkansas leading to a multiple day period of severe weather.
episodes.214336: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the Brevard County coast.
episodes.214444: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Storms weakened as they headed into northwest Iowa during the evening but still produced some hail up to ping-pong ball size and strong thunderstorm winds.
episodes.214466: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast and offshore produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.214510: Weak sea breeze boundaries beneath a broad and deep area of high pressure served as a focal point for convective initiation.  A warm, moist, and unstable environment allowed a few of the storms to produce severe marine wind gusts.
episodes.214567: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
episodes.214616: A line of severe storms that produced widespread wind damage in Alabama moved into southwest Georgia and gradually weakened, but not before producing a few more reports of wind damage.
episodes.214676: A stationary boundary draped across Arkansas in tandem with a high CAPE, low shear environment would set up a region of significantly high DCAPE across central and southern Arkansas. The result would be multiple reports of large hail, but mostly damaging winds, including a downburst that impact locations south-southwest of the Little Rock metro.
episodes.214727: A line of strong to severe storms organized over southwest Kentucky during the early morning hours of June 1, 2026. These storms moved south into West Tennessee and along the Tennessee River into northeast Mississippi during the morning hours. The storms fed on strong instability and adequate deep-layer shear to produce isolated wind damage and large hail. This first round of storms left behind an outflow boundary extending from eastern Arkansas across the Memphis metropolitan area into north Mississippi. Storms ignited along this boundary during the late afternoon and evening hours, fueled by strong instability and an upper-level trough overspreading the region. There were several additional reports of large hail and damaging.

episodes.214811: A broken line of thunderstorms developed in a northwest to southeast orientation across northwest Kansas during the early morning hours on the 1st and moved east to northeast. Quarter size hail was reported northwest of Goodland in Sherman county.
episodes.214813: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed and moved northeast across northwest Kansas during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 1st. Hail up to quarter size and 58 mph winds were both reported in Sherman county.
episodes.215101: Scattered thunderstorms and isolated storm clusters developed during the afternoon in advance of a cold front. Several of the storms produced damaging wind gusts along with some noteworthy hail.
episodes.215102: A severe thunderstorm developing ahead of a cold front moved south out of South Carolina into the northeast Georgia Piedmont during the afternoon. The storm produced a swath of damaging wind gusts from the western shore of Lake Hartwell into eastern Elbert County.
episodes.215147: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms moved east to northeast across east-central and northeast Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 1st. The highest wind gust was 64 mph in Yuma county, and the largest hail was one inch in diameter in Yuma and Kit Carson counties.
episodes.215599: Low pressure located near the South Carolina/Georgia state line along with deep moisture across the region led to an environment favorable for flash flooding.
episodes.215704: Severe storms developed on June 1st mostly across central and southern Mississippi as afternoon heating of a very moist airmass contributed to substantial atmospheric destabilization. The primary observed impacts were from damaging winds though at least one report of large hail was recorded. Additional thunderstorms developed in the afternoon of June 2nd in a similarly unstable summer airmass.
episodes.215754: Thunderstorms moving offshore produced gusty winds along the Space and Treasure Coasts.
episodes.216021: A convective cloud line developed near the middle and upper Florida Keys during the midday hours of June 1, 2026.  Multiple waterspouts were observed along the oceanside of the Bahia Honda Key and Islamorada vicinities.

A tornado touched down in an open field southwest of the intersection of 266th Street and 459th Avenue. The tornado moved to the east-northeast for around one minute crossing 459th Avenue and impacting a farmstead where it damaged two barns, downed several large tree limbs, and a fence. The tornado turned a bit more northeast across 266th Street before lifting in an open field to the north. The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated peak wind of 80 mph and an estimated average path width of 40 yards.

The primary circulation then broadened as the tornado turned more eastward and at times exhibited smaller brief vortices.
